sentence: A function f: R -> R is uniformly continuous on a set E if for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that |f(x) - f(y)| < epsilon whenever |x - y| < delta for x, y in E. Continuous functions on compact sets are automatically uniformly continuous, but on (0, 1) the function 1/x is continuous yet fails uniform continuity because its modulus of continuity blows up near zero.

The Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem states that if f_n -> f pointwise almost everywhere and |f_n| <= g for some integrable g, then the integral of f_n converges to the integral of f. This permits exchanging limit and integral without the strong hypothesis of uniform convergence required by the Riemann theory.

Taylor's theorem with the integral remainder writes f(x) = sum_{k=0}^{n} f^{(k)}(a)(x-a)^k / k! + (1/n!) integral_a^x (x-t)^n f^{(n+1)}(t) dt. The remainder term shows explicitly how the truncation error depends on the size of the (n+1)-th derivative on the interval between a and x.

The supremum of the set {1 - 1/n : n in N} is 1, although 1 itself is never attained. This illustrates that the completeness of the real numbers is essential: an order-theoretic least upper bound exists even when no element of the set realises it, and many existence theorems in analysis ultimately rest on this property.

If a series sum a_n converges absolutely, every rearrangement converges to the same sum. The Riemann rearrangement theorem shows that for a conditionally convergent series of real terms, one can rearrange the terms so that the partial sums approach any prescribed real number, or diverge to plus or minus infinity.

The mean value theorem asserts that for f continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there exists c in (a, b) with f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a). Applied to f(x) = log x on [1, 1+h] it yields the bound h/(1+h) <= log(1+h) <= h, a useful estimate in analytic inequalities.

A sequence (x_n) is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is N with |x_n - x_m| < epsilon for all n, m >= N. In R every Cauchy sequence converges; this is the content of the completeness axiom. In Q the sequence of decimal truncations of sqrt(2) is Cauchy yet has no rational limit, hinting at the construction of R via equivalence classes of rationals.

The fundamental theorem of calculus links differentiation and integration: if F is an antiderivative of a continuous f on [a, b], then integral_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). The deeper version says that for integrable f, the function F(x) = integral_a^x f(t) dt is differentiable almost everywhere with F'(x) = f(x), assuming f is suitably regular at x.

Fourier inversion on the circle recovers a sufficiently smooth periodic function from its Fourier coefficients: f(x) = sum_{n in Z} c_n e^{inx} with c_n = (1/2pi) integral_0^{2pi} f(t) e^{-int} dt. Convergence holds in L^2 by Parseval, pointwise by Dirichlet's theorem for piecewise C^1 functions, and uniformly when the coefficients are absolutely summable.

Compactness of [0, 1] is the engine behind the extreme value theorem. Any open cover {U_alpha} of [0, 1] admits a finite subcover, so by passing to a finite collection one can transfer local control of a continuous function into a uniform bound. Without compactness, on (0, 1) the function x -> 1/x is continuous but unbounded, and no analogue holds.

The spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices states that any A = A^T in R^{n x n} can be written as A = Q Lambda Q^T, where Q is orthogonal and Lambda is diagonal. The columns of Q are an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and the diagonal entries of Lambda are the corresponding real eigenvalues. This decomposition underlies principal component analysis and the analysis of quadratic forms.

Let A be an m x n matrix. The rank-nullity theorem asserts dim(ker A) + dim(im A) = n. Equivalently, the dimension of the solution space of Ax = 0 plus the dimension of the column space equals the number of columns. The result follows by extending a basis of the kernel to a basis of R^n and tracking images under A.

The determinant of a triangular matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries, and the determinant is multiplicative: det(AB) = det(A) det(B). Combined with the LU decomposition A = LU with L unit lower triangular and U upper triangular, this gives det(A) = product of pivots, providing both a computational route and the conceptual link between invertibility and nonzero determinant.

Given an inner product space, the Gram-Schmidt process orthonormalises a basis v_1, ..., v_n by setting u_1 = v_1/||v_1|| and inductively u_k = (v_k - sum_{j<k} <v_k, u_j> u_j) / ||...||. The procedure realises the QR factorisation of the matrix whose columns are the v_k and is numerically improved by the modified Gram-Schmidt variant.

The singular value decomposition writes A = U Sigma V^T with U, V orthogonal and Sigma diagonal with nonnegative entries sigma_1 >= ... >= sigma_r > 0. The columns of V are an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A^T A with eigenvalues sigma_i^2, and AV_i = sigma_i U_i. Truncating at rank k yields the best rank-k approximation in both Frobenius and operator norm.

Jordan normal form classifies square matrices over an algebraically closed field up to similarity. Every A in C^{n x n} is similar to a block-diagonal matrix whose blocks are Jordan blocks J(lambda, k) consisting of lambda on the diagonal and 1 above. The sizes of the blocks for eigenvalue lambda encode the dimensions of generalised eigenspaces ker (A - lambda I)^j.

Two vector subspaces U, W of V satisfy dim(U + W) = dim U + dim W - dim(U cap W). When U cap W = {0} the sum is called direct, written U oplus W, and every vector in U oplus W has a unique decomposition u + w. This identity is the linear-algebraic shadow of the inclusion-exclusion principle.

A linear map T: V -> W between finite-dimensional spaces is injective if and only if ker T = {0}, and is surjective if and only if dim(im T) = dim W. If dim V = dim W then injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity are all equivalent, generalising the elementary fact that a square matrix is invertible iff Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.

The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial: if p(t) = det(tI - A), then p(A) = 0 as a matrix. One slick proof uses the adjugate matrix identity (tI - A) adj(tI - A) = p(t) I and reads coefficients of powers of t, but the result also follows from the Jordan form by direct computation on Jordan blocks.

The trace of a matrix is invariant under similarity transformations and equals the sum of eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity. Combined with the identity tr(AB) = tr(BA) for compatible matrices, this implies that no finite-dimensional operators A, B satisfy [A, B] = AB - BA = I, since the trace of the right-hand side would be n while that of the left is zero.

Fermat's little theorem says that for any prime p and integer a coprime to p, a^{p-1} ≡ 1 (mod p). Equivalently a^p ≡ a (mod p) holds for all integers a. The result underpins primality tests such as the Miller-Rabin algorithm and the security analysis of RSA-style cryptosystems.

The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd(a, b) by iterating (a, b) -> (b, a mod b) until the second component is zero. Bezout's identity extracts integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b) from the back-substitution of the algorithm, and these x, y give the inverse of a modulo b when gcd(a, b) = 1.

A finite field exists for every prime power q = p^n and is unique up to isomorphism. Its multiplicative group F_q^* is cyclic of order q - 1, generated by a primitive element. Polynomials over F_q split completely in F_{q^d} for some d, and the Frobenius endomorphism x -> x^p generates the Galois group of F_{q^n}/F_q.

The Chinese remainder theorem provides a ring isomorphism Z/mn ≅ Z/m x Z/n when gcd(m, n) = 1. Given residues a (mod m) and b (mod n) one reconstructs x (mod mn) by writing x = a n n^{-1} + b m m^{-1}, where the inverses are computed modulo m and n respectively.

Lagrange's theorem in finite group theory states that the order of any subgroup H of a finite group G divides the order of G. In particular, the order of any element divides |G|. Applied to (Z/p)^* it gives Fermat's little theorem, and applied to (Z/n)^* it gives Euler's generalisation a^{phi(n)} ≡ 1 (mod n) for gcd(a, n) = 1.

Quadratic reciprocity asserts that for distinct odd primes p, q the Legendre symbols satisfy (p/q)(q/p) = (-1)^{((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2)}. Combined with the supplementary laws giving (-1/p) and (2/p), it yields an efficient algorithm for deciding whether an integer is a quadratic residue modulo a prime.

An ideal I of a commutative ring R is prime if R/I is an integral domain, and maximal if R/I is a field. In Z the ideals are exactly the (n), and (n) is prime iff n is 0 or a prime, maximal iff n is prime. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz extends this correspondence to polynomial rings over an algebraically closed field.

The Sylow theorems classify the p-subgroups of a finite group G of order p^a m with gcd(p, m) = 1. A subgroup of order p^a, called a Sylow p-subgroup, always exists; all Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate; and their number n_p satisfies n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) and n_p divides m. These constraints often force normality, simplifying classification problems.

The ring of Gaussian integers Z[i] is a Euclidean domain under the norm N(a + bi) = a^2 + b^2. A prime p of Z remains prime in Z[i] iff p ≡ 3 (mod 4); otherwise p factors as a product of conjugate Gaussian primes. This explains which primes are sums of two squares: precisely those congruent to 1 (mod 4), together with 2.

Galois theory establishes a correspondence between intermediate fields of a finite separable extension L/K and subgroups of Gal(L/K). Normal extensions correspond to normal subgroups, and the degree [L:K] equals the order of the Galois group. The classical insolvability of the general quintic follows from the non-solvability of S_5.

The linear ODE y' + p(x) y = q(x) is solved by multiplying through by the integrating factor mu(x) = exp(integral p(x) dx), turning the left-hand side into (mu y)'. Integrating yields y(x) = (1/mu(x)) (integral mu(t) q(t) dt + C), valid wherever p and q are continuous and mu is nonzero.

A second-order linear ODE y'' + p(x) y' + q(x) y = 0 has solution space of dimension two. If y_1 is one solution, reduction of order via y_2 = u(x) y_1 produces a first-order ODE for u' whose integration yields a linearly independent companion. The Wronskian W(y_1, y_2) satisfies Abel's identity W' = -p W and thus never vanishes if it is nonzero at one point.

Picard's existence and uniqueness theorem guarantees a unique local solution to y' = f(x, y), y(x_0) = y_0 whenever f is continuous and Lipschitz in y on a neighbourhood. The proof uses the Banach fixed point theorem applied to the integral operator T phi(x) = y_0 + integral_{x_0}^x f(t, phi(t)) dt on a small enough time interval.

The heat equation u_t = D u_{xx} on the real line has fundamental solution G(x, t) = (4 pi D t)^{-1/2} exp(-x^2 / (4 D t)). The solution with initial data u_0 is given by convolution u(x, t) = (G(., t) * u_0)(x), exhibiting the instantaneous infinite-speed smoothing that distinguishes the parabolic regime from the hyperbolic wave equation.

A two-dimensional autonomous system dx/dt = f(x, y), dy/dt = g(x, y) is linearised at an equilibrium (x_*, y_*) by computing the Jacobian J = [[f_x, f_y], [g_x, g_y]] there. The trace and determinant of J classify the equilibrium as node, spiral, saddle, or centre, with stability determined by the sign of trace and discriminant.

Sturm-Liouville theory studies eigenvalue problems -(p y')' + q y = lambda w y with separated boundary conditions. Under standard hypotheses the eigenvalues form an increasing sequence lambda_n -> infinity, the eigenfunctions are orthogonal in the weighted L^2 sense, and they form a complete basis for expanding sufficiently regular functions.

The Poincare-Bendixson theorem constrains the long-term behaviour of a planar flow: a bounded forward orbit of a smooth C^1 vector field must approach an equilibrium, a periodic orbit, or a heteroclinic cycle. The result rests on the Jordan curve theorem and fails in three or more dimensions, where chaotic attractors become possible.

Lyapunov's direct method establishes stability of an equilibrium x_* without solving the ODE explicitly: if there is V with V(x_*) = 0, V(x) > 0 nearby, and dV/dt = grad V . f <= 0 along trajectories, then x_* is stable, and strict negativity gives asymptotic stability. Choosing V is part craft, part inspiration from physical energy.

The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system dx/dt = a x - b x y, dy/dt = -c y + d x y admits the conserved quantity H(x, y) = d x - c log x + b y - a log y on the positive quadrant. Trajectories are level curves of H, giving the characteristic out-of-phase oscillations of predator and prey populations.

Lorenz's system dx/dt = sigma(y - x), dy/dt = x(rho - z) - y, dz/dt = x y - beta z exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions for sigma = 10, beta = 8/3, rho = 28. Its strange attractor has Hausdorff dimension approximately 2.06 and provided the first low-dimensional model of deterministic chaos in a physical context.

If X_1, ..., X_n are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2, the central limit theorem states that sqrt(n)(bar X_n - mu)/sigma converges in distribution to the standard normal. The result holds under quite weak conditions and provides the theoretical foundation for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests built around sample means.

Bayes' theorem rewrites a posterior in terms of prior and likelihood: P(theta | x) = P(x | theta) P(theta) / P(x). The marginal P(x) = integral P(x | theta) P(theta) d theta is typically the analytically intractable piece, but cancels in MCMC samplers such as Metropolis-Hastings, which only require ratios of unnormalised densities.

A random variable X has moment generating function M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]. When M_X exists in a neighbourhood of 0 it determines the distribution uniquely, and its k-th derivative at 0 equals the k-th moment E[X^k]. For independent X, Y the product M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y, which gives slick proofs that sums of independent normals are normal.

The law of total variance decomposes Var(Y) = E[Var(Y | X)] + Var(E[Y | X]). The first term measures within-group variability, the second measures between-group variability. The decomposition is central to ANOVA, to the analysis of mixed models, and to understanding shrinkage estimators in empirical Bayes problems.

A Markov chain on a finite state space with transition matrix P has stationary distribution pi satisfying pi P = pi. If the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, pi is unique and the chain converges to pi from any starting distribution; this is the ergodic theorem underlying MCMC sampling and PageRank-style algorithms.

Maximum likelihood estimation chooses theta to maximise the log-likelihood l(theta) = sum log f(x_i; theta). Under regularity conditions the MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal with covariance matrix I(theta)^{-1}, where I is the Fisher information matrix; Cramer-Rao gives the corresponding lower bound on unbiased estimators.

A confidence interval at level 1 - alpha for a parameter theta is a random set C(X) with the property P_theta(theta in C(X)) >= 1 - alpha for every theta. The frequentist interpretation refers to long-run coverage over repeated sampling, not to a probability statement about theta given the observed data; Bayesian credible intervals provide the latter.

Brownian motion B_t is a continuous Gaussian process with independent increments, B_0 = 0, and Var(B_t - B_s) = t - s. Its paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable, and (B_t)^2 - t is a martingale. Ito's lemma extends the chain rule to functions of Brownian paths, adding a (1/2) f''(B_t) dt correction term arising from quadratic variation.

The chi-squared distribution with k degrees of freedom is the distribution of Z_1^2 + ... + Z_k^2 where Z_i are iid standard normals. It has mean k and variance 2k. The Pearson statistic sum (O_i - E_i)^2 / E_i for a contingency table is asymptotically chi-squared under the null of independence.

Conditional expectation E[X | F] with respect to a sigma-algebra F is the L^2-best F-measurable predictor of X. It is uniquely defined up to almost-sure equality and satisfies the tower property E[E[X | F] | G] = E[X | G] whenever G is a sub-sigma-algebra of F. These properties make conditional expectation the cornerstone of martingale theory.

A holomorphic function f on a connected open set U is determined by its values on any set with an accumulation point inside U. This identity theorem follows from the fact that the zero set of a non-constant holomorphic function consists of isolated points, since near any zero the Taylor expansion factors as (z - z_0)^k g(z) with g(z_0) nonzero.

Cauchy's integral formula expresses f(z_0) = (1/(2 pi i)) oint_gamma f(z)/(z - z_0) dz whenever f is holomorphic inside and on a simple closed contour gamma enclosing z_0. Differentiating under the integral sign yields f^{(n)}(z_0) = (n!/(2 pi i)) oint_gamma f(z)/(z - z_0)^{n+1} dz, so holomorphicity automatically implies infinite differentiability.

The residue theorem evaluates oint_gamma f(z) dz = 2 pi i sum Res(f, z_k), summed over poles z_k enclosed by gamma. For the rational function 1/(z^2 + 1) on a large semicircle in the upper half plane, the only enclosed pole is z = i with residue 1/(2i), yielding the real integral integral_{-infty}^{infty} dx/(x^2 + 1) = pi.

Liouville's theorem states that a bounded entire function is constant. From it, the fundamental theorem of algebra follows in a single line: if a polynomial p of positive degree had no complex root, then 1/p would be entire and bounded, forcing it to be constant and contradicting deg p >= 1.

The Riemann mapping theorem asserts that any simply connected proper open subset of C is conformally equivalent to the open unit disk. The map is unique once one fixes the image of an interior point and the argument of the derivative there. The boundary behaviour is captured by Caratheodory's extension theorem when the boundary is a Jordan curve.

An isolated singularity of f at z_0 is removable, a pole, or essential. The Casorati-Weierstrass theorem says that near an essential singularity, f takes values arbitrarily close to every complex number. Picard's great theorem strengthens this dramatically: f attains every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often in every neighbourhood of z_0.

The function zeta(s) = sum_{n >= 1} n^{-s} converges for Re(s) > 1 and admits meromorphic continuation to all of C with a simple pole at s = 1 of residue 1. The functional equation zeta(s) = 2^s pi^{s-1} sin(pi s/2) Gamma(1-s) zeta(1-s) relates values at s and 1 - s, with the critical line Re(s) = 1/2 lying at the symmetry axis.

The argument principle counts zeros and poles inside a contour: (1/(2 pi i)) oint_gamma f'(z)/f(z) dz = Z - P, where Z and P are zeros and poles inside gamma counted with multiplicity. Rouche's theorem leverages this to compare zero counts of f and f + g when |g| < |f| on gamma, a standard tool for locating roots of perturbed polynomials.

Conformal maps preserve angles and the orientation thereof. The Mobius transformation T(z) = (az + b)/(cz + d) with ad - bc nonzero permutes the extended complex plane and sends circles and lines to circles and lines. Three points determine a Mobius transformation, so any three distinct points can be mapped to any three distinct target points.

Harmonic functions on a domain in C are real parts of holomorphic functions locally; equivalently they satisfy Laplace's equation Delta u = 0. The mean value property u(z_0) = (1/(2 pi)) integral_0^{2 pi} u(z_0 + r e^{i theta}) d theta characterises harmonicity, and the maximum principle prevents non-constant harmonic functions from attaining interior maxima.

A topological space X is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. For metric spaces this is equivalent to sequential compactness and to being complete and totally bounded. Tychonoff's theorem states that an arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology, and the proof for uncountable products requires the axiom of choice.

The fundamental group pi_1(X, x_0) consists of homotopy classes of loops based at x_0 under concatenation. For the circle S^1 the group is isomorphic to Z, classified by winding number. For the torus T^2 it is Z x Z, and for the figure-eight wedge S^1 v S^1 it is the free group on two generators, which is non-abelian.

Brouwer's fixed point theorem says that every continuous map f: D^n -> D^n from the closed n-disk to itself has at least one fixed point. The proof uses the fact that the n-sphere is not a retract of the n+1-disk, which itself follows from a homology computation showing that the boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism that no retract could exist alongside.

The Euler characteristic of a finite CW complex is the alternating sum of cell counts chi = sum (-1)^k c_k. It is a homotopy invariant equal to the alternating sum of Betti numbers. For an orientable closed surface of genus g, chi = 2 - 2g, recovering chi(S^2) = 2 and chi(T^2) = 0 immediately.

A space is connected if it cannot be written as the disjoint union of two non-empty open sets. Path-connectedness is strictly stronger in general, as shown by the topologist's sine curve, whose closure is connected but not path-connected. For open subsets of R^n the two notions coincide.

Singular homology H_n(X) is defined as the n-th homology of the chain complex generated by continuous maps from the n-simplex into X. The Mayer-Vietoris sequence relates the homology of X = U union V to the homologies of U, V, and U cap V via a long exact sequence, providing a computational engine for spaces glued from simpler pieces.

The classification of compact surfaces without boundary states that every such surface is homeomorphic to either S^2, a connected sum of g tori for some g >= 1, or a connected sum of k projective planes for some k >= 1. The two non-orientable families coincide modulo connected sum with one extra projective plane to a torus.

A covering map p: tilde X -> X is a continuous surjection such that each x in X has a neighbourhood U with p^{-1}(U) a disjoint union of sets each mapped homeomorphically onto U. Subgroups of pi_1(X) correspond bijectively to connected coverings of X up to isomorphism, the universal cover corresponding to the trivial subgroup.

The Banach-Tarski paradox decomposes a solid ball in R^3 into five pieces that can be rearranged by rigid motions into two solid balls of the same radius. The pieces are non-measurable in the Lebesgue sense; the construction uses the axiom of choice and the non-amenability of the free group on two generators acting by rotations.

Urysohn's lemma asserts that in a normal topological space, any two disjoint closed sets A, B can be separated by a continuous function f: X -> [0, 1] with f = 0 on A and f = 1 on B. This is the key technical tool for the Tietze extension theorem, which extends continuous real-valued functions from closed subspaces.

The binomial coefficient C(n, k) counts the k-element subsets of an n-element set and satisfies Pascal's identity C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k). Summing across a row of Pascal's triangle gives sum_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) = 2^n, and the alternating sum sum (-1)^k C(n, k) vanishes for n >= 1.

The principle of inclusion-exclusion computes |A_1 union ... union A_n| = sum |A_i| - sum |A_i cap A_j| + ... + (-1)^{n+1} |A_1 cap ... cap A_n|. Applied to counting derangements, it gives D_n = n! sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k / k!, with D_n / n! approaching 1/e as n grows.

The generating function for the Fibonacci numbers F_n is sum F_n x^n = x / (1 - x - x^2). Partial fractions give a closed form F_n = (phi^n - psi^n) / sqrt(5), where phi = (1 + sqrt(5))/2 and psi = (1 - sqrt(5))/2 are the roots of t^2 - t - 1 = 0. The asymptotic F_n ~ phi^n / sqrt(5) follows immediately.

Ramsey's theorem guarantees that for any k and r there exists N = R(k, r) such that every 2-colouring of the edges of K_N contains a monochromatic complete subgraph on k vertices in one of r colours. The values are notoriously hard to pin down; R(5, 5) is known only to lie between 43 and 48 despite decades of search.

A partition of an integer n is a weakly decreasing sequence of positive integers summing to n. The number p(n) has generating function product_{k >= 1} 1/(1 - x^k). Euler showed that the number of partitions of n into distinct parts equals the number into odd parts, with bijective proof via the identity 1 - x^{2k} = (1 - x^k)(1 + x^k).

Catalan numbers C_n = C(2n, n)/(n+1) count binary trees on n internal nodes, triangulations of a convex (n+2)-gon, lattice paths from (0,0) to (n,n) staying weakly below the diagonal, and parenthesisations of n+1 factors. The recurrence C_{n+1} = sum_{k=0}^{n} C_k C_{n-k} reflects splitting at a root.

The number of permutations of {1, ..., n} with exactly k cycles is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind, c(n, k). The recurrence c(n+1, k) = n c(n, k) + c(n, k-1) records whether n+1 is inserted into an existing cycle or starts a new one. Summing over k recovers n! by counting permutations both ways.

A Latin square of order n is an n x n array filled with n symbols so each symbol appears exactly once in each row and column. Two Latin squares are orthogonal if their superposition produces every ordered pair exactly once. Euler conjectured no pair of orthogonal Latin squares of order 4k + 2 exists, but Bose, Shrikhande, and Parker disproved this in 1959 for all such n except 6.

Polya's enumeration theorem counts orbits of a group action on coloured arrangements via the cycle index. For necklaces of n beads in k colours under rotation by the cyclic group C_n, the number of distinct necklaces is (1/n) sum_{d | n} phi(n/d) k^d, where phi is Euler's totient function.

Bell numbers B_n count partitions of an n-element set into unlabeled non-empty subsets. They satisfy the recurrence B_{n+1} = sum_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) B_k and have the elegant exponential generating function sum B_n x^n / n! = exp(e^x - 1). The first few values are 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203.

An undirected graph G is Eulerian if and only if it is connected and every vertex has even degree, in which case it admits a closed walk traversing each edge exactly once. Hierholzer's algorithm constructs such a tour in linear time by greedily extending and splicing in subtours from unvisited edges.

The chromatic polynomial P(G, k) counts proper k-colourings of G and satisfies the deletion-contraction recurrence P(G, k) = P(G - e, k) - P(G / e, k) for any edge e. For the complete graph K_n it evaluates to k(k-1)(k-2)...(k-n+1), and for trees on n vertices it is k(k-1)^{n-1}.

The four colour theorem asserts that every planar graph admits a proper colouring with at most four colours. First proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 using a computer to check a discharging argument over 1936 reducible configurations, the result resisted attempts at a purely human-verifiable proof for over a century.

A graph G is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd cycle. Equivalently, V(G) can be partitioned into two independent sets. Konig's theorem states that in any bipartite graph, the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover, which fails for general graphs as shown by the triangle K_3.

Dijkstra's algorithm computes single-source shortest paths in a graph with non-negative edge weights in O((V + E) log V) using a Fibonacci heap. The greedy invariant is that at each step the vertex with the smallest tentative distance has been finalised; this fails with negative edges, where Bellman-Ford in O(VE) is required.

The max-flow min-cut theorem of Ford and Fulkerson establishes that in any flow network the maximum value of an s-t flow equals the minimum capacity of an s-t cut. Each augmenting path along a residual graph improves the flow until none remains, at which point the saturated edges define a minimum cut.

A planar graph satisfies Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 for its drawing on the sphere. Combined with the constraint 3F <= 2E for simple planar graphs without triangles, this gives E <= 3V - 6, immediately proving that K_5 and K_{3,3} are non-planar; Kuratowski's theorem says these are the only obstructions up to subdivision.

The spectral gap of a regular graph, namely lambda_1 - lambda_2 between the first and second eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix, controls the mixing rate of random walks. Expander graphs maintain a constant spectral gap as the graph grows, leading to fast mixing, robust connectivity, and applications across pseudorandomness and error-correcting codes.

Turan's theorem gives the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph that avoids K_{r+1}, namely (1 - 1/r) n^2 / 2 asymptotically. The extremal graph is the complete r-partite Turan graph T(n, r) with parts as equal in size as possible; deviating from balance strictly reduces the edge count.

A tournament is a directed graph in which exactly one of (u, v) or (v, u) is present for every pair of distinct vertices. Every tournament contains a Hamiltonian path, by a short induction on the number of vertices. Strongly connected tournaments additionally contain a Hamiltonian cycle, by a 1959 result of Camion.

Newton's method for finding a root of f iterates x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n). Near a simple root the convergence is quadratic: |x_{n+1} - r| <= C |x_n - r|^2 for some constant C depending on the second derivative. Quadratic convergence roughly doubles the number of correct digits per iteration once close enough to r.

Gaussian quadrature with n nodes integrates polynomials of degree up to 2n - 1 exactly on [-1, 1] when the nodes are the zeros of the Legendre polynomial P_n and the weights are w_i = 2/((1 - x_i^2)(P_n'(x_i))^2). This is optimal among interpolatory rules with n nodes, far exceeding the degree-n - 1 exactness of equal-spaced Newton-Cotes formulas.

The condition number kappa(A) = ||A|| ||A^{-1}|| measures the sensitivity of the linear system Ax = b to perturbations in b. A relative perturbation of size epsilon in b can produce a relative change up to kappa(A) epsilon in x. For the Hilbert matrix H_{ij} = 1/(i + j - 1) the condition number grows roughly as (1 + sqrt(2))^{4n} / sqrt(n), so n = 10 is already disastrous in double precision.

Runge-Kutta methods integrate the ODE y' = f(t, y) by combining evaluations of f at several intermediate points within each step. The classical fourth-order RK4 method has local truncation error O(h^5) and global error O(h^4), and serves as the workhorse for non-stiff initial value problems where adaptive stepsize control further improves efficiency.

The QR algorithm finds eigenvalues of a real matrix by iterating A_k = Q_k R_k followed by A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k, which is similar to A_k. With shifts and reduction to Hessenberg form first, the cost per eigenvalue is O(n^2) and the iteration converges cubically with the Wilkinson shift, making it the standard algorithm in LAPACK.

Conjugate gradient solves a symmetric positive definite system Ax = b in at most n steps in exact arithmetic, but is typically run as an iterative method with stopping criterion ||r_k|| < tol ||b||. The convergence rate after k steps is bounded by 2 ((sqrt(kappa) - 1)/(sqrt(kappa) + 1))^k times the initial error, where kappa is the condition number.

Floating-point arithmetic following IEEE 754 represents real numbers as sign x mantissa x 2^exponent within finite precision. Double precision provides about 15.95 decimal digits. Catastrophic cancellation occurs when subtracting nearly equal quantities; for example, computing 1 - cos x naively near zero loses many digits, but rewriting as 2 sin^2(x/2) restores accuracy.

Spline interpolation through n + 1 data points (x_i, y_i) uses piecewise cubic polynomials with matching first and second derivatives at interior knots. The natural spline additionally imposes vanishing second derivatives at the endpoints, yielding a tridiagonal linear system for the second derivatives at the knots that is solvable in O(n) operations.

The fast Fourier transform computes the discrete Fourier transform of a length-N vector in O(N log N) operations, in contrast to the naive O(N^2) matrix multiplication. The Cooley-Tukey algorithm splits a transform of length 2N into two transforms of length N plus N twiddle-factor multiplications, exploiting symmetries of the N-th roots of unity.

Backward error analysis shows that Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting computes the exact factorisation of a slightly perturbed matrix A + E, with ||E|| <= n^2 g_n epsilon_machine ||A||. The growth factor g_n is typically modest in practice though it can in principle reach 2^{n-1}; this distinction between worst-case and observed behaviour is the heart of practical linear-system stability.

Godel's first incompleteness theorem shows that any consistent, recursively axiomatised theory T extending Peano arithmetic admits a sentence G_T that is true in the standard model but unprovable in T. The proof constructs G_T as a sentence asserting its own unprovability in T, using a coding of formulas as natural numbers and a fixed-point lemma.

The compactness theorem of first-order logic states that a set of sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset has one. From it follow striking consequences: nonstandard models of arithmetic containing infinite natural numbers; nonstandard reals containing infinitesimals; and the inability of first-order logic to characterise finiteness.

The Lowenheim-Skolem theorem says that any first-order theory with an infinite model has models of every infinite cardinality. In particular, ZFC has countable models despite proving the existence of uncountable sets; this Skolem paradox is resolved by noting that uncountability is relative to the model's interpretation of bijection.

Cantor's diagonal argument shows that there is no surjection from N to the power set P(N). Suppose f: N -> P(N) and consider D = {n in N : n not in f(n)}; if f(m) = D, then m in D iff m not in f(m) = D, a contradiction. The same construction generalises to show |X| < |P(X)| for every set X.

A theory T is said to be complete if for every sentence phi in its language, either T proves phi or T proves not phi. The theory of dense linear orders without endpoints is complete and decidable; the theory of arithmetic on the integers is neither, by Godel's theorems and the undecidability of Diophantine equations established by Matiyasevich.

The halting problem is undecidable: there is no algorithm that, given a Turing machine M and input w, correctly determines whether M halts on w. The proof reduces to a diagonal contradiction by considering the behaviour of a putative decider on its own encoding. Rice's theorem extends this to show that no non-trivial semantic property of programs is decidable.

The continuum hypothesis asserts that there is no set whose cardinality lies strictly between |N| and |R|. Godel showed CH is consistent with ZFC by constructing the constructible universe L, and Cohen showed not-CH is also consistent by introducing forcing. Together these establish that CH is independent of ZFC.

Modal logic extends classical propositional logic with operators Box and Diamond, read as necessity and possibility. Kripke semantics interprets Box phi at a world w as truth of phi at every world accessible from w. The system S4 axiomatises reflexive transitive accessibility relations and matches the topological interpretation of Box as interior on a topological space.

Tarski's undefinability theorem proves that arithmetical truth is not definable within arithmetic: there is no formula T(x) such that for every sentence phi the equivalence T(corner phi corner) <-> phi is provable in the theory. This is a sibling result to Godel's incompleteness theorems and rests on the same self-referential machinery.

The completeness theorem of first-order logic, due to Godel in 1929, says that the formal proof system is sound and complete with respect to the semantics: a sentence is provable from a set of axioms if and only if it is true in every model of the axioms. This contrasts with the incompleteness theorems by clarifying what completeness can and cannot achieve.

A category C consists of a class of objects, a class of morphisms with domain and codomain, an associative composition, and an identity morphism on each object. Functors F: C -> D map objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms preserving composition and identities. Natural transformations are morphisms of functors, fillings of commutative naturality squares.

Yoneda's lemma states that for a functor F: C^op -> Set and any object X, the natural transformations from the representable functor Hom(-, X) to F are in bijection with F(X). The contravariant version gives the embedding C -> Fun(C^op, Set) sending X to Hom(-, X), which is fully faithful, justifying that objects are determined by their morphism sets.

Adjoint functors F: C -> D and G: D -> C satisfy Hom_D(F X, Y) iso Hom_C(X, G Y), natural in X and Y. The free-forgetful pair from sets to groups is the prototype: the free group functor is left adjoint to the underlying-set functor. Limits commute with right adjoints, colimits with left adjoints.

A limit of a diagram D: J -> C is a universal cone, an object L equipped with morphisms L -> D(j) compatible with the morphisms of J. Products are limits over discrete categories, equalisers are limits over a parallel-arrow category, and pullbacks are limits over a span. A category is complete if all small limits exist.

Monads on a category C are endofunctors T: C -> C equipped with a unit eta: 1 -> T and multiplication mu: T T -> T satisfying associativity and unit axioms. Every adjunction gives rise to a monad, and conversely every monad is induced by an adjunction with its Eilenberg-Moore category. In functional programming, monads model effects such as state, exceptions, and I/O.

An object X in C is initial if there is exactly one morphism from X to every object, and terminal if there is exactly one morphism from every object to X. In Set the empty set is initial and any singleton is terminal; in the category of groups the trivial group is both, an example of a zero object characteristic of pointed and abelian categories.

An abelian category satisfies axioms making it suitable for homological algebra: every morphism has kernel and cokernel, monomorphisms are kernels and epimorphisms are cokernels, and the natural map from coimage to image is an isomorphism. The category of modules over a ring is abelian, as is the category of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space.

Pullback squares characterise fibre products. Given f: A -> C and g: B -> C, the pullback A times_C B consists of pairs (a, b) with f(a) = g(b), together with projections to A and B. In Top the pullback realises the topological fibre product, and in Set it is simply the subset of A x B satisfying the equation f(a) = g(b).

Kan extensions provide the most universal way to extend a functor F: C -> E along a functor K: C -> D. The left Kan extension Lan_K F satisfies a coend formula (Lan_K F)(d) = integral^{c in C} Hom_D(K c, d) tensor F c, and represents the best left-approximation to extending F. They underlie many constructions in homotopy theory.

A topos is a category resembling the category of sets, with finite limits, exponentials, and a subobject classifier Omega. Every Grothendieck topos arises as sheaves on a site; the elementary topos axioms isolate the categorical content. Internal logic in a topos is intuitionistic, with the subobject lattice replacing the boolean algebra of subsets.

A sigma-algebra on X is a collection F of subsets containing the empty set, closed under complementation, and closed under countable unions. A measure mu: F -> [0, infty] satisfies mu(empty) = 0 and countable additivity. The Borel sigma-algebra on R is generated by the open intervals and is strictly smaller than the Lebesgue sigma-algebra.

Lebesgue measure on R is the unique translation-invariant Borel measure assigning length b - a to every interval (a, b). Its construction via the Caratheodory extension of outer measure produces a complete sigma-algebra strictly larger than Borel, containing every subset of a null set. Vitali's construction exhibits non-measurable sets assuming the axiom of choice.

Fubini's theorem permits exchanging the order of integration in a double integral provided either the function is non-negative or its integral is absolutely convergent. The hypothesis matters: without integrability, sum_{(m, n)} a_{m, n} can yield different values depending on summation order, as in the textbook example where the matrix has alternating row and column sums.

The Radon-Nikodym theorem states that if mu and nu are sigma-finite measures on (X, F) with nu absolutely continuous with respect to mu, then there exists a measurable function f >= 0 with nu(E) = integral_E f d mu for every E in F. The density f is unique mu-almost everywhere and is denoted d nu / d mu.

The Lebesgue differentiation theorem says that for a locally integrable f on R^n, the average (1/|B_r(x)|) integral_{B_r(x)} f(y) dy tends to f(x) for almost every x as r tends to 0. The Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality controls the maximal averages and is the principal tool behind the proof.

Egorov's theorem says that if f_n -> f almost everywhere on a finite measure space, then for every epsilon > 0 there is a measurable set E with mu(E^c) < epsilon on which f_n -> f uniformly. The result fails for sigma-finite measures with unbounded total mass and is a useful bridge between pointwise and uniform convergence.

The Cantor set C is constructed by iteratively removing middle thirds from [0, 1]. It is uncountable, compact, totally disconnected, and has Lebesgue measure zero. Its Hausdorff dimension is log 2 / log 3 approximately 0.631, demonstrating that compact sets of measure zero can carry rich fractal structure measured by dimension rather than length.

Jensen's inequality says that for a convex function phi and a random variable X with finite expectation, phi(E[X]) <= E[phi(X)]. Reversing for concave phi recovers an upper bound. The inequality is the source of many classical bounds, including AM-GM and the entropy version of Gibbs' inequality in information theory.

The space L^p(X, mu) for p in [1, infty) consists of measurable f with integral |f|^p d mu < infty modulo almost-everywhere equality, normed by ||f||_p = (integral |f|^p d mu)^{1/p}. Holder's inequality gives ||fg||_1 <= ||f||_p ||g||_q for 1/p + 1/q = 1, and Minkowski's inequality establishes the triangle inequality for ||.||_p.

A signed measure on (X, F) decomposes uniquely as nu = nu^+ - nu^- by the Hahn-Jordan decomposition, with nu^+ and nu^- mutually singular positive measures. The total variation |nu| = nu^+ + nu^- defines a norm under which the space of finite signed measures becomes a Banach space, dual to C_0(X) for X locally compact Hausdorff via Riesz representation.

A Banach space is a complete normed vector space. The Hahn-Banach theorem extends a bounded linear functional from a subspace to the whole space without increasing its norm. Three classical consequences are the existence of nonzero continuous functionals on any nontrivial Banach space, the separation of disjoint convex sets, and the embedding of X into its double dual X^**.

The Banach-Steinhaus theorem, also known as the uniform boundedness principle, states that a family of bounded linear operators T_alpha: X -> Y between Banach spaces with sup_alpha ||T_alpha x|| < infty for every x in X is uniformly bounded: sup_alpha ||T_alpha|| < infty. The proof uses Baire category to find a small ball on which the operators are uniformly bounded.

The open mapping theorem says that a surjective bounded linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is open: T(U) is open in Y whenever U is open in X. Equivalently, T has a bounded right inverse on every closed subspace complement. The closed graph theorem follows as a corollary, asserting that a linear T with closed graph is bounded.

A Hilbert space H comes with an inner product whose induced norm makes H complete. Every closed convex subset of H contains a unique element of minimum norm; specialising to a closed subspace gives the orthogonal projection. The Riesz representation theorem identifies H with its dual via the conjugate-linear map y -> <-, y>.

A bounded operator T on a Hilbert space H is compact if T maps bounded sets to relatively compact sets. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators says T = sum lambda_n <e_n, .> e_n, with eigenvalues lambda_n -> 0 and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors e_n. This generalises the diagonalisation of symmetric matrices to infinite dimensions.

The weak topology on a Banach space X is the coarsest topology making every functional in X^* continuous. By Banach-Alaoglu, the closed unit ball of X^* is compact in the weak-* topology. In reflexive spaces the unit ball is also weakly compact, providing the principal compactness tool for nonlinear variational problems.

Distributions, or generalised functions, are continuous linear functionals on the space of test functions C_c^infty(R^n). Differentiation is defined by transposition: (T', phi) = -(T, phi'). Every locally integrable function defines a distribution by integration, and the Dirac delta is the distribution sending phi to phi(0); its derivatives sense local fluctuations of phi at the origin.

Fredholm theory studies operators T = I - K with K compact on a Banach space. The Fredholm alternative says that either T is invertible, or its kernel and the kernel of T^* have equal finite dimensions and span the orthogonal complements of im T^* and im T respectively. The index ind(T) = dim ker T - dim coker T is zero for I - K.

A Banach algebra is a Banach space with a compatible associative multiplication. The Gelfand transform sends a commutative unital Banach algebra A to C(M_A), where M_A is the space of maximal ideals with the weak-* topology. For A = L^1(R) with convolution, the transform recovers the Fourier transform, embedding the algebra into C_0(R-hat).

The spectrum sigma(T) of a bounded operator T on a Banach space is the set of complex lambda for which T - lambda I is not invertible. It is compact and non-empty when X is over C. The spectral radius is given by r(T) = lim ||T^n||^{1/n}, which coincides with the maximum modulus of points in sigma(T) by Gelfand's formula.

The wave equation u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx} on R has general solution u(x, t) = F(x - ct) + G(x + ct) by d'Alembert. Initial data u(x, 0) = phi(x), u_t(x, 0) = psi(x) determine F and G via F(x) = (phi(x) - (1/c) integral_0^x psi)/2 and G correspondingly, recovering d'Alembert's classical formula.

Laplace's equation Delta u = 0 has harmonic solutions satisfying the mean value property and the maximum principle. The Dirichlet problem on a bounded domain with continuous boundary data has a unique classical solution when the domain has a sufficiently regular boundary. Perron's method constructs solutions as suprema of subharmonic functions matching the prescribed boundary values.

Sobolev space H^1(Omega) consists of L^2 functions with weak derivatives in L^2. The Sobolev embedding H^1(Omega) hookrightarrow L^{2n/(n-2)}(Omega) for n >= 3 controls higher Lebesgue norms by Dirichlet energy and underlies existence theory for nonlinear elliptic PDEs via direct methods of the calculus of variations.

The method of characteristics solves quasilinear first-order PDEs by reducing to a system of ODEs along characteristic curves. For the inviscid Burgers equation u_t + u u_x = 0 the characteristics are dx/dt = u, dt = 1, and information propagates at the local speed u. Initial profiles with negative slope develop shocks in finite time t = -1/min u_x(x, 0).

The Schrodinger equation i partial_t psi = -(hbar^2 / 2m) Delta psi + V psi governs the time evolution of quantum states. Spectral methods diagonalise the Hamiltonian H = -(hbar^2 / 2m) Delta + V; for the harmonic oscillator V = m omega^2 x^2 / 2 the eigenvalues are hbar omega (n + 1/2) and the eigenfunctions are Hermite functions.

Energy estimates control solutions to evolution PDEs without explicit formulas. For the heat equation, multiplying u_t = Delta u by u and integrating yields (1/2) d/dt ||u||_{L^2}^2 + ||grad u||_{L^2}^2 = 0, immediately giving decay of the L^2 norm and an integrated control on the Dirichlet energy.

Weak solutions to elliptic PDEs are defined via integration by parts against test functions. For -Delta u = f in Omega with u = 0 on partial Omega, a weak solution u in H_0^1 satisfies integral grad u . grad phi = integral f phi for every phi in H_0^1. Lax-Milgram guarantees existence and uniqueness when the bilinear form is coercive.

The Navier-Stokes equations u_t + (u . grad) u = -grad p + nu Delta u, div u = 0 model viscous incompressible fluid flow. Existence of smooth global solutions in three spatial dimensions for arbitrary smooth initial data is one of the Clay Millennium Problems, with no resolution despite Leray's weak existence theory from 1934.

Hyperbolic conservation laws u_t + f(u)_x = 0 admit weak entropy solutions characterised by Lax's entropy condition or Kruzkov's entropy pairs. For scalar laws on R, Kruzkov's theorem establishes uniqueness in the class of bounded measurable functions of bounded variation, with L^1-contraction between initial profiles.

Separation of variables for the heat equation u_t = u_{xx} on (0, L) with u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0 gives eigenmodes u_n(x, t) = sin(n pi x / L) exp(-(n pi / L)^2 t). Initial data are expanded in Fourier sine series, and the time evolution is term-by-term exponential decay, with the slowest modes dominating long-time behaviour.

An affine variety V(I) in A^n_k is the zero set of an ideal I in k[x_1, ..., x_n]. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz states that over an algebraically closed field, the maximal ideals of k[x_1, ..., x_n] correspond to points of A^n_k, and the radical of an ideal equals the intersection of the maximals containing it.

Projective space P^n_k parametrises lines through the origin in A^{n+1}_k. A projective variety is the common zero set of homogeneous polynomials, and projective morphisms between projective varieties are closed maps. This compactness property underlies Bezout's theorem: two plane curves of degrees d_1 and d_2 with no common component meet in exactly d_1 d_2 points counted with multiplicity.

Elliptic curves over a field of characteristic neither 2 nor 3 admit the Weierstrass form y^2 = x^3 + a x + b with discriminant -16(4 a^3 + 27 b^2) nonzero. The set of k-rational points forms an abelian group under the chord-tangent law, with the point at infinity as identity. Mordell's theorem says this group is finitely generated over Q.

A scheme is locally the spectrum Spec A of a commutative ring, with structure sheaf and Zariski topology. Grothendieck's formulation subsumes classical varieties, arithmetic objects such as Spec Z, and infinitesimal thickenings used to define formal moduli. Functor of points encodes a scheme by Hom(Spec R, X), often more convenient than direct manipulation of the structure sheaf.

The genus of a smooth projective curve C over an algebraically closed field is the dimension of the space of regular differentials H^0(C, Omega_C). Genus 0 curves are isomorphic to P^1, genus 1 curves are elliptic, and higher genus curves admit hyperbolic structure. Riemann-Roch computes h^0(D) - h^0(K - D) = deg D - g + 1 for any divisor D on C.

A line bundle L on a projective variety X has Picard group Pic(X) classifying such bundles up to isomorphism. Its degree on a curve C inside X equals the intersection number L . C, and the canonical bundle K_X comes from the top exterior power of the cotangent sheaf. Ampleness of L means high tensor powers embed X into projective space.

Resolution of singularities for an algebraic variety X over a field of characteristic zero is a proper birational morphism Y -> X with Y smooth. Hironaka's 1964 theorem establishes existence by a sequence of blow-ups along smooth centres. The corresponding question in positive characteristic remains open in dimensions above three.

Sheaf cohomology H^i(X, F) measures the obstruction to extending local sections of a sheaf F to global ones. For projective varieties X over a field, H^i(X, F) is finite-dimensional, and Serre duality identifies H^i(X, F) with H^{n-i}(X, F^vee tensor K_X)^vee for F locally free and X smooth of dimension n.

The Zariski topology on A^n_k is the coarsest in which polynomials are continuous, with closed sets the zero loci of ideals. It is very non-Hausdorff: any two non-empty open sets in an irreducible variety intersect. Irreducible algebraic sets correspond bijectively to prime ideals, and the dimension equals the Krull dimension of the coordinate ring.

A toric variety is built from a fan of rational cones in a lattice. Each cone sigma corresponds to an affine toric variety Spec k[sigma-check cap M], and these are glued along common faces. The combinatorial structure of the fan controls geometric invariants: smoothness corresponds to the cones being generated by parts of bases, and properness corresponds to the support of the fan covering the full vector space.

A smooth manifold M is locally homeomorphic to R^n via charts whose transition maps are smooth. The tangent space T_p M at a point p is the vector space of derivations on smooth functions at p, with dimension equal to dim M. The disjoint union of tangent spaces forms the tangent bundle TM with its natural smooth structure.

A Riemannian metric g on M assigns smoothly to each point an inner product on the tangent space. Length of a curve gamma: [a, b] -> M is the integral of sqrt(g(gamma', gamma')) dt. Geodesics minimise length locally and satisfy the geodesic equation D/dt gamma' = 0 in terms of the Levi-Civita connection.

Gauss's Theorema Egregium states that the Gaussian curvature of a surface in R^3 depends only on the intrinsic metric, not on the embedding. The curvature is invariant under bending without stretching, which explains why a flat piece of paper cannot be wrapped onto a sphere without tearing or compressing.

The Gauss-Bonnet theorem for a closed oriented Riemannian surface says integral_M K dA = 2 pi chi(M), where K is the Gaussian curvature and chi(M) is the Euler characteristic. The integrated curvature is a topological invariant: bending a sphere never changes the integrated curvature from 4 pi, even though the local curvature varies.

A connection on a vector bundle E -> M provides a notion of parallel transport along curves and induces a covariant derivative nabla: Gamma(E) -> Gamma(T^* M tensor E). The curvature F = nabla nabla measures the failure of parallel transport around small loops to return to identity; its components are the Riemann curvature tensor in the Levi-Civita case.

A symplectic form on a 2n-dimensional manifold is a closed nondegenerate 2-form omega. By Darboux's theorem, near any point there are coordinates p_i, q_i in which omega = sum dp_i wedge dq_i, so symplectic manifolds have no local invariants beyond the dimension. Hamiltonian flows preserve omega and provide the geometric setting for classical mechanics.

Lie groups are smooth manifolds carrying a compatible group structure. The Lie algebra g of G is the tangent space at the identity, equipped with the bracket [X, Y] arising from the commutator of left-invariant vector fields. The exponential map exp: g -> G is a local diffeomorphism near 0, and for matrix groups coincides with the matrix exponential.

Stokes' theorem on a smooth oriented manifold with boundary says integral_M d omega = integral_{partial M} omega. Specialisations recover the fundamental theorem of calculus on intervals, Green's theorem on plane regions, the classical Stokes' theorem on surfaces in R^3, and the divergence theorem for 3-dimensional regions.

A Kahler manifold is a complex manifold equipped with a Hermitian metric whose associated 2-form omega is closed. The metric, complex structure, and symplectic form are compatible and any two determine the third. Compact Kahler manifolds enjoy Hodge decomposition: H^k(M, C) splits as direct sum of H^{p, q}(M) with p + q = k, providing strong constraints on their topology.

Geodesic equations on the upper half-plane with the Poincare metric g = (dx^2 + dy^2)/y^2 are vertical lines and semicircles meeting the real axis perpendicularly. The Gaussian curvature is identically -1, making it a model of hyperbolic geometry. Triangles have angle sum strictly less than pi, with defect equal to the hyperbolic area.

Shannon entropy H(X) = -sum p(x) log p(x) measures the average uncertainty of a discrete random variable. It is maximised at log |X| for the uniform distribution and minimised at 0 for a point mass. The base of the logarithm sets the unit: bits for base 2, nats for base e, hartleys for base 10.

Shannon's source coding theorem says that a discrete memoryless source of entropy H bits per symbol can be losslessly compressed to H bits per symbol on average, but not below. Huffman coding achieves the minimum average length L satisfying H <= L < H + 1 for any source with finite alphabet, by greedy bottom-up merging of the two least-likely symbols.

The channel capacity C of a noisy channel is the supremum over input distributions of the mutual information I(X; Y). Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem says that rates below C are achievable with vanishing error probability through block coding, while rates above C have error probability bounded away from zero asymptotically.

Mutual information I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X | Y) = H(Y) - H(Y | X) is symmetric and non-negative, vanishing if and only if X and Y are independent. It equals the Kullback-Leibler divergence D(p(x, y) || p(x) p(y)) between the joint and product distributions, geometrically the divergence of the joint from the independence model.

Fano's inequality bounds the error probability of any estimator hat X of X from observation Y: H(X | Y) <= 1 + P_e log(|X| - 1). Hence small conditional entropy forces small error probability and vice versa, providing converses for the channel coding theorem and many estimation-theoretic problems.

Kullback-Leibler divergence D(p || q) = sum p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)) is non-negative, with equality iff p = q, by Jensen's inequality applied to the convex function -log. It is not a metric: it is asymmetric and fails the triangle inequality. Despite this, it is the canonical statistical distance between distributions and underlies the EM and variational inference algorithms.

Differential entropy h(X) = -integral f(x) log f(x) dx of a continuous random variable can be negative and is not invariant under change of variables: a linear scaling X -> a X shifts h by log |a|. The Gaussian distribution maximises differential entropy among densities with fixed variance sigma^2, attaining h = (1/2) log(2 pi e sigma^2).

The Gaussian channel Y = X + Z with Z normal of variance N and an input power constraint E[X^2] <= P has capacity C = (1/2) log(1 + P/N) per use. The capacity-achieving input distribution is Gaussian with variance P, and the resulting Y is Gaussian with variance P + N, so the entropic geometry is exactly soluble.

Linear block codes [n, k, d] encode k information bits as n codeword bits with minimum distance d. The Hamming bound states 2^k sum_{i=0}^{t} C(n, i) <= 2^n for codes correcting t = floor((d-1)/2) errors. Codes saturating the bound are called perfect; the Hamming codes [2^m - 1, 2^m - m - 1, 3] are the canonical examples.

Arithmetic coding losslessly compresses a sequence by associating it with a subinterval of [0, 1) whose length equals the probability of the sequence under the model. Iterative subdivision according to symbol probabilities zeroes in on a number that, in binary, requires approximately -log_2 P bits to specify, matching the entropy bound asymptotically.

Convex optimisation minimises convex functions over convex sets. A local minimum is automatically global, and first-order optimality conditions are sufficient as well as necessary. KKT conditions extend Lagrange multipliers to inequality constraints: at an optimum the gradient of the objective equals a non-negative linear combination of active constraint gradients, with complementary slackness.

Gradient descent minimises a differentiable function by iterating x_{k+1} = x_k - eta grad f(x_k). For an L-smooth convex f and step size eta = 1/L, the suboptimality decreases as f(x_k) - f^* <= 2 L ||x_0 - x^*||^2 / k. Strong convexity with parameter mu accelerates convergence to a linear rate (1 - mu/L)^k.

Linear programming maximises a linear functional c^T x subject to A x <= b and x >= 0. The simplex method walks along edges of the polyhedral feasible region from vertex to vertex, improving the objective. Interior point methods follow a central path through the relative interior and provably solve LPs in polynomial time, while simplex remains exponential in the worst case.

Duality in linear programming pairs primal max c^T x : A x <= b, x >= 0 with dual min b^T y : A^T y >= c, y >= 0. Weak duality says primal optimum <= dual optimum always, and strong duality says equality holds whenever either is finite. Complementary slackness characterises pairs of optimal primal-dual solutions.

Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a random subsample at each step. For convex Lipschitz objectives with bounded gradient noise, the iterate average achieves O(1/sqrt(k)) suboptimality, slower than full-batch O(1/k) but dramatically cheaper per step. Variance reduction techniques such as SVRG recover linear convergence under strong convexity assumptions.

Lagrangian duality replaces a constrained minimisation min f(x) s.t. g(x) <= 0 with the unconstrained Lagrangian L(x, lambda) = f(x) + lambda^T g(x). The dual function q(lambda) = inf_x L(x, lambda) is concave in lambda. Maximising q over lambda >= 0 lower-bounds the primal; equality holds for convex problems under Slater's regularity condition.

Newton's method for unconstrained minimisation uses x_{k+1} = x_k - (grad^2 f(x_k))^{-1} grad f(x_k) and converges quadratically near a strict local minimum where the Hessian is positive definite. Quasi-Newton variants such as BFGS approximate the inverse Hessian by rank-2 updates, retaining superlinear convergence without explicit second derivative computation.

Semidefinite programming optimises a linear functional over the cone of positive semidefinite matrices subject to linear constraints. It generalises linear programming and admits polynomial-time interior point algorithms. Many combinatorial relaxations including Goemans-Williamson's 0.878-approximation for MAX CUT are obtained by lifting boolean variables to vectors and solving the resulting SDP.

Subgradients generalise gradients to convex non-differentiable functions: g is a subgradient of f at x if f(y) >= f(x) + g^T (y - x) for all y. The set of subgradients at x is the subdifferential. Subgradient descent x_{k+1} = x_k - eta_k g_k with eta_k = O(1/sqrt(k)) achieves O(1/sqrt(k)) convergence for Lipschitz convex objectives.

Dynamic programming solves multistage decision problems by backward recursion on a value function. Bellman's principle of optimality says that an optimal policy from any state has optimal continuation. For deterministic finite-horizon problems with N stages and S states, the value iteration computes the optimal cost in O(N S^2) operations by tabulating one-step transitions.

A strategic game has players, strategies, and payoff functions. A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile in which no player can improve by unilateral deviation. Nash's theorem guarantees existence of an equilibrium in mixed strategies for every finite game, via Kakutani's fixed point theorem applied to the best-response correspondence.

The prisoner's dilemma demonstrates the gap between individually rational and collectively optimal behaviour. With payoffs T > R > P > S and constraint 2 R > T + S, mutual defection is the unique Nash equilibrium although mutual cooperation strictly Pareto dominates. Repeated play allows cooperative equilibria sustained by punishment strategies such as tit-for-tat.

Zero-sum two-player games admit a value v by von Neumann's minimax theorem: v = max_x min_y x^T A y = min_y max_x x^T A y over mixed strategies x, y. The optimal mixed strategies and the value are computable by linear programming, with the primal and dual LPs corresponding to the two players' problems.

Cooperative game theory studies coalitions of players sharing a transferable utility. The Shapley value phi_i(v) = sum_S (|S|! (n - |S| - 1)! / n!)(v(S cup {i}) - v(S)) is the unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, dummy, and additivity. It averages each player's marginal contribution over all orderings of arrivals.

Mechanism design seeks rules that implement social objectives under strategic agent behaviour. The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism for combinatorial auctions charges each winning bidder the externality imposed on others, making truth-telling a dominant strategy. The revelation principle says that without loss of generality one can restrict attention to direct mechanisms in which agents report types truthfully.

Stable matching for the marriage problem with n men and n women always exists, by the Gale-Shapley deferred-acceptance algorithm. Men propose in rounds of preference and women hold the best proposal received so far. The algorithm terminates in at most n^2 rounds and produces the man-optimal stable matching, with the women receiving their worst stable partner.

Evolutionary game theory studies stable strategies under replicator dynamics dx_i/dt = x_i ((A x)_i - x^T A x), where x_i is the population fraction playing strategy i. Evolutionary stable strategies are local attractors and characterise stable mixed-strategy equilibria robust to invasion by rare mutants. Hawk-dove and rock-paper-scissors are textbook examples of distinct dynamic regimes.

Auction theory analyses bidding behaviour in environments with private information. In a sealed-bid second-price auction (Vickrey), bidding one's true valuation is a weakly dominant strategy. Revenue equivalence says that under symmetric private values, any auction allocating the item to the highest valuation and giving zero surplus to the lowest type yields the same expected revenue.

Bayesian games incorporate private types theta_i drawn from a prior. A Bayes-Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile sigma_i(theta_i) such that each type plays a best response given the conditional distribution over others' types. The Harsanyi transformation reduces a game of incomplete information to one of imperfect information with an explicit nature move.

Repeated games support a much wider set of equilibria than their one-shot counterparts. The folk theorem says that for infinitely repeated games with sufficiently patient players, any feasible individually-rational payoff vector arises as a subgame-perfect equilibrium. Discount factors close to 1 enable elaborate punishment-and-reward strategies that sustain cooperation.

The Weierstrass elliptic function wp(z) attached to a lattice L satisfies the differential equation (wp')^2 = 4 wp^3 - g_2 wp - g_3, where g_2 and g_3 are the Eisenstein series of weights 4 and 6. It is doubly periodic, meromorphic on C, and has a double pole at every lattice point with principal part 1/z^2 near the origin.

The modular discriminant Delta(tau) = (2 pi)^{12} eta(tau)^{24} is a cusp form of weight 12 for the full modular group SL(2, Z), where eta is the Dedekind eta function. It vanishes nowhere on the upper half-plane and its q-expansion sum tau(n) q^n defines the Ramanujan tau function, whose multiplicativity tau(mn) = tau(m) tau(n) for coprime m, n was proved via Hecke operators.

A modular form of weight k for SL(2, Z) is a holomorphic function f on the upper half-plane satisfying f((a tau + b)/(c tau + d)) = (c tau + d)^k f(tau) for every integer matrix of determinant 1, with f holomorphic at the cusp. The graded ring of all such forms is the polynomial ring C[E_4, E_6] generated by the Eisenstein series of weights 4 and 6.

The j-invariant j(tau) = E_4^3 / Delta is a modular function of weight 0 that defines a bijection between the quotient of the upper half-plane by SL(2, Z) and the complex plane. Two elliptic curves over C are isomorphic precisely when they share the same j-invariant, so j parametrises isomorphism classes of complex tori.

The Jacobi theta function theta_3(z, q) = sum_{n in Z} q^{n^2} e^{2 pi i n z} satisfies the heat-like functional equation and transforms under tau -> -1/tau by the Jacobi imaginary transformation theta_3(0, -1/tau) = sqrt(-i tau) theta_3(0, tau). Its zeros and quasi-periodicity encode the addition theorems for elliptic functions.

Every elliptic function with periods omega_1 and omega_2 is a rational function of wp and wp'. The sum of residues over a fundamental parallelogram vanishes, so no nonconstant elliptic function has a single simple pole; the minimal order of a nonconstant elliptic function is two, realised by wp itself.

The Eisenstein series E_{2k}(tau) = 1 - (4k / B_{2k}) sum_{n >= 1} sigma_{2k-1}(n) q^n is a modular form of weight 2k for k >= 2, where B_{2k} is a Bernoulli number and sigma is a divisor sum. The weight-2 case E_2 fails strict modularity, transforming with an extra term and giving rise to the quasimodular forms.

The dimension of the space of cusp forms of weight k for SL(2, Z) is zero for k < 12 and odd k, and otherwise grows linearly with k. The valence formula, counting zeros of a weight-k form in a fundamental domain as k/12, forces this dimension count and explains why Delta is the unique normalised cusp form of weight 12.

Hecke operators T_n act on the space of modular forms of weight k and commute with each other. A normalised eigenform for all T_n has q-expansion coefficients that coincide with its eigenvalues and are multiplicative. The associated L-function L(f, s) = sum a_n n^{-s} then factors as an Euler product over primes.

The lemniscatic elliptic function arises from the lattice of Gaussian integers and inverts the arc length integral of the lemniscate of Bernoulli. Gauss discovered that its real period equals 2 varpi where varpi = 2 integral_0^1 dt / sqrt(1 - t^4), and that the lemniscate can be divided into n equal arcs by ruler and compass exactly when n is a Fermat-type product.

Van der Waerden's theorem asserts that for every pair of positive integers r and k there exists W(r, k) such that any r-colouring of the integers from 1 to W(r, k) contains a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length k. The proof proceeds by a double induction on k and the number of colours, producing towering but finite bounds.

Schur's theorem states that for any finite colouring of the positive integers there exist monochromatic x, y, z with x + y = z. The proof colours edges of a complete graph on vertices labelled by integers, where the edge between i and j inherits the colour of |i - j|, and invokes the finite Ramsey theorem to find a monochromatic triangle.

The Hales-Jewett theorem says that for any finite alphabet of size t and any number of colours r there is a dimension H(t, r) such that every r-colouring of the cube of side t in dimension H(t, r) contains a monochromatic combinatorial line. Van der Waerden's theorem follows by projecting combinatorial lines onto arithmetic progressions.

The probabilistic lower bound for diagonal Ramsey numbers shows R(k, k) > 2^{k/2}. Colour each edge of the complete graph on n vertices independently; the expected number of monochromatic k-cliques is C(n, k) 2^{1 - C(k,2)}, and when this is below 1 a good colouring exists, giving the exponential lower bound by Erdos's deletion-free first-moment argument.

The infinite Ramsey theorem states that for any finite colouring of the k-element subsets of an infinite set, there is an infinite subset all of whose k-element subsets share one colour. The case k = 2 with two colours is the pigeonhole-flavoured statement that any 2-colouring of edges of the infinite complete graph contains an infinite monochromatic clique.

The Erdos-Szekeres theorem guarantees that any sequence of more than (r-1)(s-1) distinct real numbers contains either an increasing subsequence of length r or a decreasing subsequence of length s. Assigning each term the pair of lengths of its longest monotone runs and applying the pigeonhole principle to those pairs yields the bound directly.

Rado's theorem characterises which systems of linear equations are partition regular: a matrix A defines a system solvable monochromatically under every finite colouring of the integers if and only if A satisfies the columns condition, meaning its columns can be partitioned into blocks each summing into the span of the preceding ones.

The Gallai-Witt theorem, the multidimensional van der Waerden statement, asserts that any finite colouring of the lattice Z^d contains a monochromatic homothetic copy of every finite configuration. Taking the configuration to be an arithmetic progression on a coordinate axis recovers the one-dimensional theorem as a special case.

The Ramsey number R(3, k) grows like k^2 / log k up to constants, by a 1995 theorem combining the upper bound of Ajtai, Komlos and Szemeredi with a matching random-graph lower bound. The off-diagonal asymptotics thus differ sharply from the still-unknown exponential growth of the diagonal numbers R(k, k).

The canonical Ramsey theorem of Erdos and Rado handles colourings with unboundedly many colours: for any colouring of the pairs from an infinite set there is an infinite subset on which the colouring is one of four canonical types, namely constant, depending only on the smaller index, only the larger, or injective. No such finite-type list exists without passing to the canonical reduction.

The Jones polynomial V(L) of an oriented link L is a Laurent polynomial in t^{1/2} defined through the Kauffman bracket and a writhe correction. It satisfies the skein relation t^{-1} V(L_+) - t V(L_-) = (t^{1/2} - t^{-1/2}) V(L_0), where L_+, L_-, L_0 differ at a single crossing, and it distinguishes the trefoil from its mirror image.

The Alexander polynomial Delta(t) of a knot is computed from a Seifert matrix V by Delta(t) = det(V - t V^T), normalised up to units to satisfy Delta(t) = Delta(t^{-1}) and Delta(1) = 1. It detects the genus of a knot from below via the degree bound and vanishes for no knot, though it fails to distinguish certain mutant pairs.

Reidemeister's theorem states that two knot diagrams represent the same knot if and only if one is obtained from the other by a finite sequence of the three Reidemeister moves together with planar isotopy. Any invariant of knots can therefore be verified by checking invariance under these three local moves alone.

The knot group, the fundamental group of the complement of a knot in the 3-sphere, is a complete invariant for prime knots up to mirror image by a theorem of Gordon and Luecke. A Wirtinger presentation reads one generator per arc of a diagram and one relation per crossing, and abelianising the group always yields the integers.

A Seifert surface of a knot is an orientable surface in the 3-sphere having the knot as its boundary. Seifert's algorithm constructs one from any diagram by smoothing all crossings and capping the resulting circles with bands. The minimal genus over all Seifert surfaces is the genus of the knot, an additive invariant under connected sum.

The bridge number of a knot counts the minimal number of local maxima in a height function on a diagram. Two-bridge knots admit a clean classification by rational numbers p/q via Schubert's normal form, and the trefoil and figure-eight are the simplest examples, having bridge number two and crossing numbers three and four respectively.

The HOMFLY polynomial is a two-variable invariant simultaneously generalising the Jones and Alexander polynomials. It is determined by the skein relation a P(L_+) - a^{-1} P(L_-) = z P(L_0) together with the normalisation P(unknot) = 1. Specialising the variables a and z recovers each of the one-variable invariants as a slice.

A knot is amphichiral if it is isotopic to its mirror image. The figure-eight knot is amphichiral, which can be confirmed because its Jones polynomial is invariant under t -> t^{-1}, whereas the trefoil's Jones polynomial is not, proving the trefoil is chiral and distinct from its reflection.

Khovanov homology assigns to each link a bigraded chain complex whose graded Euler characteristic recovers the Jones polynomial. This categorification is a strictly finer invariant: it detects the unknot, a fact proved by Kronheimer and Mrowka, and distinguishes pairs of knots that the Jones polynomial alone cannot separate.

The linking number of a two-component link is half the signed count of crossings between the two components, and is invariant under all Reidemeister moves. For the Hopf link it equals plus or minus one, certifying that the two circles cannot be pulled apart, while the Whitehead link has linking number zero yet remains nontrivially linked.

The p-adic absolute value of a nonzero rational a = p^n u/v with u, v coprime to p is |a|_p = p^{-n}. It satisfies the strong triangle inequality |x + y|_p <= max(|x|_p, |y|_p), and Ostrowski's theorem shows that every nontrivial absolute value on Q is equivalent either to the usual one or to some p-adic one.

The field Q_p of p-adic numbers is the completion of Q with respect to the p-adic metric. Every element has a unique expansion sum_{n >= -k} a_n p^n with digits a_n in {0, ..., p-1}, and a series converges in Q_p precisely when its general term tends to zero, a dramatic simplification of the convergence theory familiar from the reals.

The ring of p-adic integers Z_p is the inverse limit of the finite rings Z/p^n Z. It is compact, equals the closed unit ball {|x|_p <= 1} of Q_p, and is a local ring with unique maximal ideal p Z_p. Its residue field Z_p / p Z_p is the finite field with p elements.

Hensel's lemma lifts a simple root of a polynomial modulo p to a root in Z_p: if f(a) is congruent to 0 modulo p while f'(a) is a unit, then there is a unique alpha in Z_p with f(alpha) = 0 and alpha congruent to a modulo p. The proof is a p-adic Newton iteration whose quadratic convergence is automatic in the ultrametric setting.

The p-adic exponential series sum x^n / n! converges only on the disk |x|_p < p^{-1/(p-1)} because the factorials in the denominators carry growing powers of p. Outside this disk the series diverges, so the p-adic exponential has a strictly bounded domain, unlike its everywhere-convergent real counterpart.

A function f from Z_p to Q_p is continuous if and only if it is the uniform limit of its Mahler expansion f(x) = sum_{n >= 0} c_n binomial(x, n), where the coefficients c_n tend to zero. Mahler's theorem thus gives an explicit orthonormal basis for the Banach space of continuous p-adic functions on Z_p.
